items.title: Build: A Front-Porch Digest for One Block
items.summary: A starter build: fork Front Porch Forum's constitution, not its code — real names, one geography, one email a day, a rotating neighbor-moderator.
items.body:
Front Porch Forum's software is proprietary, but its constitution is four rules, and the studied effects (members more likely to volunteer, attend local events, and talk to neighbors) flow from the rules, not the code. Build the rules:

1. **Real names, real addresses.** Members are verified neighbors — by the moderator knowing them, which at block scale is the whole verification system.
2. **One geography.** This digest serves these three blocks. There is no 'nearby areas' toggle. Growth means helping the next three blocks start their own.
3. **One send a day.** Posts queue; the digest goes out at 6pm; nothing is urgent by design. (Actual emergencies have actual channels.)
4. **A human moderator.** A neighbor — rotating quarterly so it stays a chore shared, not a fiefdom — reads everything before it ships, and knows the difference between a hard conversation and a harmful one.

The build: a submission form (email-in works too), a queue the moderator approves, a daily digest email, and a public archive page. Posts are the FPF genre mix: borrowed ladders, lost cats, contractor recommendations, meeting announcements, thanks.

Constraint: resist every feature that makes it faster. The pace is the product. If a neighbor asks for push notifications, the correct response is a porch conversation.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Front Porch Forum
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: the pace is the product — one send a day
growth means seeding new digests, not expanding this one

items.title: Build: Phone-First Mutual Aid Intake
items.summary: A starter build: the Bed-Stuy Strong pattern at pod scale — a phone number in front, a claimable ticket board behind, and data minimization as a founding principle.
items.body:
Build the intake-and-dispatch layer for a small mutual aid network, honoring the two hardest-won lessons of the COVID networks.

**Phone-first.** The front door is a phone number (voice and text) plus a paper flyer that says so. A web form exists but is the secondary door. Every request — 'a week of groceries,' 'ride to the pharmacy,' 'someone to shovel' — becomes a ticket with a rough location (block, not address, until claimed), needs, and language preference.

**A claimable board.** Volunteers see open tickets near them and claim one — the Bed-Stuy Strong mechanic that made 30 deliveries a day feel human: one neighbor takes responsibility for one neighbor, start to finish, with a check-in when it's done.

**Data minimization as architecture, not policy.** Collect only what fulfillment needs; addresses visible only to the claiming volunteer; tickets auto-purge after completion; export is a decision two stewards make together, not a button. The COVID networks learned that a spreadsheet of vulnerable neighbors is a liability to protect, not an asset to grow — design as if the least trustworthy future volunteer will someday have the password.

Dashboard: open needs, average time-to-claim, and thanks — read aloud at the monthly meeting, because the ledger of care is also a story of us.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Bed-Stuy Strong & MAMAS
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: phone number in front, app in back

items.title: Build: A Third-Places Map for Your Neighborhood
items.summary: A starter build: a local Ushahidi — neighbors collectively map the porches, stoops, cafés, courts, and corners where the neighborhood actually happens, with stories attached to every pin.
items.body:
Ushahidi is a global open-source platform for crowdsourced mapping; this build borrows its soul at block scale. Make a map where neighbors pin the third places of one neighborhood — the spots that are neither home nor work where life actually happens: the good stoop, the café that lets you sit, the pickup court, the library steps, the taco truck corner, the community fridge.

Each pin carries a neighbor's words: what happens here, when it's alive, who you'll meet, one story. Submissions are moderated by a named neighbor-steward (the Ushahidi lesson: every good deployment has one). Views: the map itself; a 'alive right now' filter by time of day; and a printable one-pager for the laundromat corkboard — because the neighbors who most need third places may not be on the map's own third place, the internet.

Extra credit: a 'missing places' layer — where neighbors mark the third place that *should* exist ('this vacant lot wants to be a plaza') — which quietly becomes an organizing map: each cluster of wishes is a constituency waiting for a first meeting.

Constraint: map conditions and places, never people — no 'suspicious activity' layers, ever. That road leads somewhere neighborhoods regret.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Ushahidi
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: map places and conditions, never people
a printable path for offline neighbors

items.title: Build: Adopt-a-Thing for Your Block
items.summary: A starter build: the Adopt-a-Hydrant pattern, remixed — a map of small civic objects (tree wells, storm drains, benches, little libraries) that neighbors claim, name, and care for.
items.body:
In 2011, Code for America fellow Erik Michaels-Ober built Adopt-a-Hydrant for Boston: a simple map where residents claimed a fire hydrant to shovel out after snowstorms — and named them. The pattern got remixed within months: storm drains, tsunami sirens in Honolulu. The insight wasn't hydrants; it was that *small civic objects + personal claim + a name* turns maintenance into relationship.

Build it for your block: a map of the things that need a person — tree wells that need summer watering, storm drains that need leaf-clearing before rain, a bench that needs paint, the little free library that needs restocking. A neighbor taps one, adopts it, names it ('Drainy McDrainface has a steward now'), and gets gentle seasonal nudges tied to real conditions (heat waves for trees, storm forecasts for drains).

Show the whole block's care at a glance: every adopted thing, every steward first-name, every 'this thing needs a person' gap. Celebrate streaks at the block party.

Constraint: adoption is an offer, not an enforcement — the tool never shames lapsed stewards, it just quietly reopens the adoption. And it works without an account for viewing; the barrier to seeing your block's care should be zero.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Erik Michaels-Ober / Code for America
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: adoption is an offer, not an enforcement
names and delight are features, not decoration

items.title: Build: Participatory Budgeting for a Very Small Budget
items.summary: A starter build: run real participatory budgeting on a block association's actual money — propose, develop, vote, do — sized so the whole cycle fits in six weeks and $500.
items.body:
Participatory budgeting usually means cities and millions. The pattern shrinks beautifully: a block association's dues, a community garden's plot fees, a mutual aid fund's surplus — anywhere neighbors hold shared money, they can decide together how to spend it.

Build the cycle at block scale: (1) **Propose** — any neighbor submits an idea with a guess at cost ('paint the fire hydrant garden', 'bulk-buy sidewalk chalk', 'a proper coffee urn for meetings'). (2) **Develop** — ideas get budget-checked by two volunteer 'delegates' and merged where they overlap; every idea gets a real cost and a named doer before it reaches the ballot. (3) **Vote** — every household gets a ballot, digital or paper, same weight; a week to vote; results public the moment polls close. (4) **Do** — winners get done, with photos posted to the same tool, closing the loop that makes people believe the next cycle.

The tool's job is legibility: anyone can see every idea, every cost, every vote count, and every receipt. Trust in tiny democracy is built by boring transparency.

Constraint: paper ballots count equally and are enterable by a steward — the neighbors with the strongest opinions about the coffee urn may never touch the app. And keep the cycle short: six weeks from first idea to finished project teaches more democracy than six months of process.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after the participatory budgeting movement
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: every winner gets done and photographed — the loop must close

items.title: Build: A Living Asset Map
items.summary: A starter build bridging both new shelves: an asset-based community development map where the assets are neighbors' own declared gifts, associations, and places — collected in conversations, not scraped.
items.body:
Asset-based community development starts from what a neighborhood has, not what it lacks: the gifts of individuals (head, hands, heart), the associations people already belong to, the institutions, the physical places, the local economy, the stories. This build gives that inventory a living home.

The map has layers: **people's gifts** (only ever self-declared or gathered in a real conversation with consent — 'Maria: sourdough, spreadsheet wizardry, listening'), **associations** (the block club, the domino regulars, the church choir — with a named connector for each), **places** (the community room nobody knows they can book, the church kitchen with the 40-quart pots), and **stories** (what this corner used to be; who to ask about it).

Its most important view isn't the map — it's the match: someone plans a repair café and the tool surfaces 'four neighbors declared fixing gifts, the church has tables, the tool library is six blocks away.' Assets that never get asked for are assets the neighborhood still doesn't have.

Constraint: this is the anti-directory. No scraping, no imports, no profiles anyone didn't write about themselves. An asset map is a gift exchange, and gifts are given, not taken. Track the asking: the map's success metric is connections made, not pins collected.

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Kretzmann & McKnight
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

guardrails: self-declared gifts only — no scraping, no involuntary profiles
success metric is connections made, not pins collected
every association gets a named human connector
